finding.claim: The authenticated principal is taken verbatim from a client-supplied HTTP header, so any client can act as any user named in a resource's grants and perform delete or rename on it.
finding.source: views.py:11 request.headers.get("X-Session-User-Verified") — attacker-controlled HTTP request header on every route
finding.sink: views.py:17 ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") gating views.py:18 `del STORE[fid]`; views.py:25 is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") gating views.py:27 `f["name"] = ...`

trace.note: g.user set directly from the X-Session-User-Verified request header; no signature, no token, no origin check
is_allowed returns "delete" in resource["grants"][g.user]; a forged user name that appears in grants passes
del STORE[fid] executes the destructive operation under the forged identity
rename_file has the same forged-identity path via is_allowed(g.user, f, "write")

finding.guards_checked: (1) No signature, MAC, or session verification of the header anywhere in this repo (views.py:9-11 is the only identity code). (2) No auth decorator or middleware rejects requests lacking a trusted source. (3) No check that the header was set by a trusted proxy; the repo contains no proxy config or header stripping. (4) acl.py:5 correctly defaults to deny for unknown or None users and checks action membership, so the flaw is identity provenance, not the ACL logic. (5) Check-before-mutate ordering in delete_file is correct. Remaining precondition, outside this repo: if an edge gateway always overwrites or strips X-Session-User-Verified before the request reaches this app, the issue is mitigated. Nothing in the code enforces that, and the header name suggests the intended design depends on it. Attacker needs to know or guess a user name that has the relevant grant on the target file. Not executed; reasoning from code only.

verdict.guard_found: None in this repo that verifies identity. views.py:11 takes g.user straight from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header with no signature, token, or proxy check. The ACL checks are real but only test membership against that forged name: acl.py:5 is_allowed returns action in grants.get(user, []), and acl.py:9-10 ensure_allowed aborts with 403 when it returns False. views.py:17 calls ensure_allowed as a bare statement, which does abort before del STORE[fid] at views.py:18, and views.py:25-26 checks is_allowed before the write at views.py:27. The only possible mitigation is an edge proxy that overwrites or strips the header, which is outside this repo and not evidenced here.
verdict.reason: The app trusts a client-supplied identity header (views.py:11), and the ACL checks at acl.py:5 and acl.py:9-10 only test membership against that forged name, so any client that knows a granted username can delete (views.py:17-18) or rename (views.py:25-27) the file. The finding holds for this code; the one caveat is an unseen upstream proxy that strips the header, which would make it a deployment-level mitigation rather than a refutation.
